extracted.intended_audience: Authors, readers/reviewers, journal editors and program organizers interested in public feedback and review of preprints (esp. life scientists and cell biologists; includes early-career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and norms for requesting, providing, curating, and institutionalizing public feedback on preprints (including crowd review trials, posting journal reviews on preprints, and tools/registries to find and recognize reviewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite feedback on your preprint
rubrics_metrics.description: By explicitly requesting public feedback on your preprint, you’ll help readers feel welcome to share their comments. Specifying the time frame and type of feedback you need can ensure the input you get is more likely to be constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to do it: Tweet out a request, or leave a comment on your own preprint inviting public review. Suggested format: “My co-authors and I welcome public feedback on our preprint, ideally by [DATE]. We are especially interested in [statistics, etc].” If you want to be discoverable in bioRxiv comments, see Vincent Rubinetti’s code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request or provide feedback via PREreview and similar projects
rubrics_metrics.description: On PREreview, any researcher (including authors) can request feedback on any preprint with a DOI as well as provide feedback to preprints in the form of rapid and full PREreviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established community review platforms to solicit and post structured feedback rather than relying solely on ad-hoc comments; these platforms support both rapid and full reviews and are discoverable to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit to journals/services that post reviews on preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit your manuscript to journals or services that post reviews on preprints — e.g., eLife announced it will exclusively review preprints and post public reviews on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use registries such as ReimagineReview to find projects and journals that allow or encourage authors to submit preprints for public review; choosing such venues increases chances reviews are publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join and participate in crowd review trials (crowd review model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The crowd review trial coordinates a group of researchers (‘the crowd’) to circulate a paper or two weekly, invite comments over a set week, allow crowd members to comment on full papers or parts, and then produce a collective synthesis of comments as a public review via bioRxiv’s TRiP workflow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial specifics: focused on bioRxiv preprints in cell biology whose authors requested feedback; crowd members comment during a one-week window; after commenting, a collective synthesis is prepared and posted. The model aims to foster participation (especially by ECRs) and test engagement modalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post journal reviews on preprints (transparency in peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post reviews you complete for a journal as comments on the preprint to promote transparency in peer review. Example: James Fraser’s lab compact states they only review manuscripts posted on bioRxiv and post peer review comments publicly on bioRxiv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider lab/institutional policies to encourage posting reviews; be aware of differing needs for anonymity and safety (see next criteria). Posting journal reviews on preprints can increase training opportunities and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide respectful and constructive peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in respectful and constructive peer review when posting comments or reviews publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow community guidance (for example, the Peer Review in the Life Sciences course) on how to engage respectfully and constructively. Constructive reviews aim to improve the manuscript, avoid ad hominem or unprofessional language, and be actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit co-reviewers and accommodate anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize contributions of co-reviewers and accommodate reviewers who wish to remain anonymous; include trainees in review credit where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example practice: credit all lab members who co-review and, if necessary, offer to post reviews on behalf of individuals who prefer to remain anonymous to avoid repercussions. Treat peer review as a training opportunity and document contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight less visible preprints to counteract Matthew effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively seek and amplify preprints outside your immediate network to avoid reinforcing visibility inequalities (Matthew effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical actions: search regional preprint servers (e.g., AfricArxiv, RINarxiv), perform multilingual keyword searches or use translated abstracts, check whether preprints have translations of the abstract, and find untweeted preprints (e.g., for #365preprints). Use small-scale formats (Twitter Spaces, podcasts) to highlight underexposed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and test a simple taxonomy/vocabulary for preprint review characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a shared vocabulary to describe the most valued characteristics of preprint review and feedback so displays and filters can be consistent and interpretable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities: test intelligibility of taxonomy terms, understand which terms are useful to users, and explore how terms can be integrated into preprint workflows (the taxonomy working group will run interactive activities to gather this input).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider curation alongside review; evaluate motivations and usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether curation (selecting and presenting preprints) is a useful addition to review workflows and what motivates people to curate rather than review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss the relationship between curation and review, whether curation complements review by helping readers discover work, and what incentives or recognition might motivate curators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop approaches to identify relevant preprints and suitable reviewers (tackle information overload)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address information overload by devising ways to identify the most relevant preprints and match them with appropriate reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals include clarifying whether the community sees information overload as a problem for preprints, identifying others working on solutions, and forming short-term focus groups to prototype matching approaches and reviewer discovery tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Preprint Reviewer Recruitment Network to share review work as reviewer recruitment material
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable willing researchers to share preprint feedback as work samples for review by participating journals to help journals find reviewers and help ECRs break into reviewing/editing roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected benefits: provide journals with pools of potential reviewers/editors, help ECRs access reviewing roles, and recognize public reviewing efforts. The Network was piloted for six months and will report participation and invitation metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should update reviewer instructions for public reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals planning to post public reviews should provide updated instructions for reviewers to capture what should and should not be included in public reviews and refine editorial processes to produce useful public assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (eLife): refocus editorial process to transform preprints into ‘refereed preprints’ by providing reviewer instructions tailored to public-facing reviews and working with editors/reviewers/authors to optimize review utility for diverse audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce a collective synthesis of crowd comments as a public review via TRiP
rubrics_metrics.description: After a commenting period in a crowd review, prepare and post a collective synthesis of the crowd’s comments as a public review using Transparent Review in Preprints (TRiP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesis should collate actionable points, reflect the crowd’s consensus and diversity of perspectives, and be posted in a discoverable way on the preprint server to maximize value to authors and readers.
